first_impression: Fused per-robot Metal kernel on a Mac, with honest MuJoCo validation. Ambitious and unusually candid about limits.
confusing: Slide 10 says 60x, then 90x, then 4x GPU and ~30x fusion; the numbers take effort to reconcile
Slide 9 walker contact diverges after 0.6-0.8 s; unclear how much that matters for training
Planar 2D only, so 'robot learning lab' oversells somewhat
doubts: 60x baseline is MuJoCo's Python mj_step loop, not tuned multithreaded C or MJX
7.6M steps/s is at 16,384 walkers but training runs at 295K steps/s
Policy transfer 19.8 vs 21.9 m is only on a MuJoCo mirror built by the same author
questions: Is the MuJoCo baseline batched, or a single-env Python loop per core?
How does the kernel handle threadgroup divergence when robots hit contacts at different times?
What stops you from fusing the PPO update, given that is 72% of the time?

fixes.change: Show one clean decomposition (4x GPU x 30x fusion = 90x vs naive CPU; 60x vs MuJoCo) as a small waterfall, and drop the second competing headline
Add a threadgroup/memory-layout diagram or a kernel excerpt with the contact solve, not just the motor line
Add a one-line takeaway on why divergence after 0.8 s does not break training, tied to the 19.8 vs 21.9 m transfer result

Slide 5: orange annotation 'motor=80 becomes a torque-speed-limited torque' runs off the right edge
Slide 14: 'MACGYM 21.9 M' label collides with the dot bar
Slides 9 and 11: dense small charts that can't be read from the back of a room
doubts: Dense text on 9, 10 and 11 undercuts the otherwise minimalist style
questions: Is the dot animation generated from the real replay data?

fixes.change: Pull the orange annotation inside the slide margin and shorten it so it does not clip
Enlarge the playground screenshot to fill the right half, and remove or label the confusing dot-tripod cluster
Move the MACGYM 21.9 M label clear of the dot bar
Show one hero chart at large size instead of six tiny ones

first_impression: A teenager made a Mac train 4,096 robots in a minute and it works live. That is genuinely insane.
confusing: Slide 5: what a Metal kernel and PPO actually are is not explained
Slide 7: the chart says 54.9 m but the lanes say 21.5 m
doubts: Built in under 4 hours solo, even with AI agents
'Robot' here is a stick figure in 2D, not a real robot
questions: Can I run this on my own MacBook right now?
How did you decide what to tell the AI agents to do?
Will you add 3D so it could drive a real arm?

fixes.change: Add a plain-English line under each step, e.g. 'Metal kernel = a tiny program that runs once per robot on the GPU'
Put a one-line note by the chart saying why 54.9 m differs from 21.5 m (training episodes are longer than the 8 s replay)
Replace the future-user text with one real thing, e.g. a screenshot of a classmate running it

first_impression: Polished and well rehearsed, but it is a solution looking for a market. Students training 2D walkers on Macs is tiny.
confusing: Who pays? 'Hosted classroom version and edu licenses' is one throwaway line
Slide 3 'Planar 2D physics, so think robot learning class, not Isaac Lab' shrinks the ambition
Slide 12 'built solo with AI agents' carries as much weight as the build itself
doubts: Zero users today, and 'DVHS CS Club' is not traction
Why a student would pick this over free Colab or MuJoCo MJX
Speed claims are against a self-chosen baseline
questions: Name one person who has run this and what they did with it
What does an RL class actually do that needs 4,096 walkers in 2D?
Why not just rent an NVIDIA GPU for a few dollars an hour?

fixes.change: Replace the vague wedge with one concrete pilot: a named teacher or club date, a count of installs, or a workshop on the calendar
Add a Colab/MJX/Isaac comparison row (offline, no quota, Mac-native, live viewer) with times
Reframe 'planar 2D' as a deliberate teaching choice rather than a disclaimer

first_impression: Slick deck, real demo, honest caveats. But I would have said the same of fifty other 'X on your laptop' projects.
confusing: Slide 2 claims 7.8 days in 1:06, then slide 6 says 3.2 days in 28 s; I had to do the math to see they match
Slide 8: the 6.16 to 2.74 m/s 'fix' looks like losing speed, not winning
Slide 11: 'not a demo, a library' is asserted but the slide is a terminal dump
doubts: Policy transfer is to a MuJoCo mirror, not hardware; 'measured' oversells it
18 checks passing in 8 commits is thin evidence of a library
Theme fit: 'ordinary' laptop is a stretch of 'elevate the ordinary'
questions: What is the single next thing that makes this not a weekend project?
How much of the hard design was yours and how much the agent's?
Why would any funder or school care?

fixes.change: Replace the terminal dump with a 20-second install-to-trained-policy proof, or lead with 'pip install works on a fresh Mac' and a test count
Add one line saying 2.74 m/s is the honest number and the real accomplishment is catching the exploit
Show the 7.8 days arithmetic once (steps x 0.02 s) so the headline claim holds up when challenged
Add a one-sentence 'what we want next' ask, such as testers or classrooms, beside the QR code
